p: There are civilisations whose memory never died: Egypt, with its pyramids standing in plain sight; Rome, whose language is still taught to every schoolboy; China, which has never ceased to read its own ancient books. And there are civilisations that were utterly forgotten, so that not even their name survived, and that had to be rediscovered by men with spades. The greatest of these is the civilisation of the valley of the Indus, in what is at present the north-west of our Indian Empire, and what the Encyclopaedia informs me will later become, after a partition of great sorrow, the country of Pakistan.

The story of its rediscovery touches my own countrymen, and not to their credit. In the eighteen fifties, the engineers building the railway between Lahore and Multan wanted ballast for the track. Near a village called Harappa they found great mounds full of ancient baked bricks, very well made, and they carried them off by the thousand and laid them under the rails. Sir Alexander Cunningham, the first Director of the Archaeological Survey of India, visited the site and found a curious small seal of stone carved with an animal and some unknown signs. He did not know what it was. Nobody did, until the nineteen twenties, when excavations at Harappa and at another great site far to the south, called Mohenjo-daro, which means, I am told, the mound of the dead, revealed that these were cities of the Bronze Age, as old as the pyramids, and belonging to a civilisation that nobody had suspected.

At its height, from about two thousand six hundred to one thousand nine hundred years before Christ, the Indus civilisation covered a larger area than either Egypt or Mesopotamia, stretching over much of what will be Pakistan and north-western India, with more than a thousand known settlements. Its cities are astonishing for their order. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were laid out on a regular plan, with broad main streets crossing at right angles and smaller lanes between. The houses were built of baked brick of standard proportions, the same across hundreds of miles. Many houses had their own wells, bathing rooms and, most remarkably, privies connected to covered drains of brick running beneath the streets, with places where they could be inspected and cleaned. Nothing so good was built in the cities of Europe until, I am almost ashamed to say, the great sewers which Sir Joseph Bazalgette has lately completed beneath the streets of London, after the Great Stink of eighteen fifty-eight drove Parliament from its own chamber.

At Mohenjo-daro there is a great tank of brick, carefully waterproofed with bitumen, which the excavators called the Great Bath and supposed to have been used for ritual washing. There are large buildings which may have been granaries or halls. There is a standard system of weights, made of polished cubes of stone, used across the whole civilisation. There is pottery, jewellery of gold and carnelian beads, toys of clay including little carts with wheels, and a small bronze figure of a dancing girl, standing with one hand on her hip in an attitude of such confident insolence that every visitor remembers her.

What there is not is equally striking. There are no great palaces, no royal tombs filled with treasure, no monuments boasting of the victories of kings. There are few weapons. Nobody knows who ruled these cities, or how. Some scholars have imagined a peaceful society governed by merchants or priests; others think that the rulers simply chose not to advertise themselves in stone. Both may be wrong.

And nobody can read their writing. The Indus people left thousands of small seals, carved with animals, most often a creature like a bull with a single horn, and with short inscriptions of a few signs. Some four hundred different signs are known. But the inscriptions are very short, there is no bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone, and the language they record is unknown. Many have claimed to decipher the script; none has persuaded the others. Some scholars even doubt that it is a full writing at all. It is one of the great unsolved puzzles of the world, and I confess I find it consoling that the men of the future, with all their engines, still cannot read it. There must be some secrets left to the dead.

The Indus cities traded widely. Their seals have been found in Mesopotamia, and the Mesopotamian texts speak of a distant land called Meluhha, from which came ivory, carnelian, timber and other precious goods, which most scholars now take to be the Indus. Ships sailed between them along the coasts of the Arabian Sea and the Persian Gulf.

From about one thousand nine hundred years before Christ, the great cities declined and were abandoned. The old explanation, which I learned as a young man in another form, was that they were destroyed by invading Aryans, the people who composed the sacred hymns called the Vedas, which speak of a god who destroys fortresses. The Encyclopaedia reports that this view has been largely abandoned for want of evidence of any conquest. The present opinion is that the climate became drier, that the rivers changed their courses, among them a great river which may be the Sarasvati of the old hymns and which dried up, and that the trade with Mesopotamia faltered. The people did not vanish; they moved east and south, into smaller villages, and their descendants are surely among the peoples of India today. Some customs, perhaps, survived: certain postures of meditation, certain ornaments, the reverence for certain animals. But the cities themselves, with their drains and their weights and their unreadable seals, were forgotten for nearly four thousand years, until an Englishman picked up a little stone with a unicorn on it, beside a railway line, and did not know what he held.
